courseLedger.name: Personal & Professional Development

contentRead.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
contentRead.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
contentRead.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
contentRead.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courseLedger.contribution: MandatoryYear1PPD,notdisciplinarycoverage.

courseLedger.name: Sustainability Essentials I

contentRead.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
contentRead.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
contentRead.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
contentRead.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

courseLedger.contribution: Sustainability Essentials I supplies physical, mathematical and systems foundations for studying linked environmental change.

courseLedger.name: Dynamic Earth

contentRead.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
contentRead.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.
contentRead.topics: Plate tectonics and the Wilson cycle; Minerals and rock formation; Volcanism and metamorphism; Sedimentation and facies; Structural deformation; Stratigraphy and palaeontology; Seismology and seismic waves; Geomagnetism and gravity; Mantle and core processes; Earth-system and climate interactions; Geological history; Geohazards
contentRead.methods: Geological field observation and measurement; Rock and mineral identification; Geological mapping and profiling; Stratigraphic-column construction; Geological cross-section construction; Sediment and facies interpretation; Geological-history reconstruction

courseLedger.contribution: Dynamic Earth directly examines structural geology, Earth history and environmental geology through laboratory and field work.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Programming

contentRead.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
contentRead.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
contentRead.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
contentRead.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

courseLedger.contribution: Introduction to Programming develops Python-based computational problem solving for environmental data and models.

courseLedger.name: Sustainability Essentials II

contentRead.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
contentRead.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
contentRead.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
contentRead.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

courseLedger.contribution: Direct wave physics, observational methods, chemical analysis and materials stress/strain connect physical evidence to environmental and resource questions; sustainability-campaign work adds critical communication, not a general Earth-system modelling course.

courseLedger.name: Mathematical Methods

contentRead.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
contentRead.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
contentRead.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
contentRead.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Develops single-variable calculus, complex numbers, integration, differential equations and analytical/Mathematica dynamic-model investigation. These are substantive Earth-system mathematical foundations; vector/matrix methods belong to the separately selected Linear Algebra course rather than this course.

courseLedger.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations

contentRead.description2: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.

courseLedger.contribution: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations applies geoscience to disasters, environmental change and adaptation.

courseLedger.name: Earth System Science Tools

contentRead.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

courseLedger.contribution: Earth System Science Tools integrates Earth-system modelling, tracers, proxies and greenhouse-gas pathways.

courseLedger.name: Climate Change

contentRead.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
contentRead.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
contentRead.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
contentRead.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

courseLedger.contribution: Climate Change directly studies anthropogenic climate change, ocean acidification and climate adaptation.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Biodiversity

contentRead.description2: The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and health.
contentRead.profile: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.
contentRead.topics: Biodiversity and its measurement; Phylogenetic relationships; Viruses; Bacteria and archaea; Protists; Fungi; Plant diversity; Invertebrates; Vertebrates and primates; Evolutionary history; Organismal ecological roles
contentRead.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Introduction to Biodiversity establishes biological diversity within the biosphere component of Earth systems.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Data Science

contentRead.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
contentRead.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
contentRead.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
contentRead.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Introduction to Data Science develops cleaning, visualisation and analysis of spatial and other datasets.

courseLedger.name: Probability & Statistics

contentRead.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
contentRead.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
contentRead.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
contentRead.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

courseLedger.contribution: Probability & Statistics develops probability, distributions and parameter estimation for environmental evidence.

courseLedger.name: Earth Observation

contentRead.description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
contentRead.profile: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
contentRead.topics: Spatial concepts and data models; Geospatial databases; Georeferencing and map projections; Spatial visualization; Spatial queries and transformations; Surface analysis; Earth-observation tools; Spectral signatures; Remote-sensing acquisition systems; Image preprocessing and processing; Environmental geospatial applications
contentRead.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design

courseLedger.contribution: Direct ArcGIS geospatial analysis, spatial data representation and surface analysis with remote-sensing/spectral acquisition and image processing; an environmental case study applies these tools. No guaranteed drone deployment or advanced temporal geostatistics.

courseLedger.name: Soils & Aquifers

contentRead.description2: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
contentRead.profile: Examines soils and shallow aquifers through soil science, environmental chemistry and applied geophysics. Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.
contentRead.topics: Soil formation, functions and taxonomy; Soil quality, amendments and threats; Soil texture, structure and aggregate stability; Soil moisture and organic matter; Soil chemistry, pH and metals; Soil biology; Sediment-cell behaviour; Shallow aquifers, salinization and freshwater interventions; Physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers; Seismology; Electrical resistivity; Electromagnetic surveying
contentRead.methods: Soil coring and field sampling; Visual soil-structure assessment (grass-VESS); Aggregate-stability, texture and sieve tests; Soil pH, moisture, organic-content and leaching analyses; Microscopy and SEM-EDS; Sample preparation for ICP/IC and interpretation of ICP results; Methylene-blue testing with spectrophotometry/titration; Seismic surveying; Electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveying; Field-data processing in Excel

courseLedger.contribution: Direct soil properties, formation, quality, salinization and field/laboratory characterization; seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate soils/aquifers. Do not infer a full groundwater-flow or freshwater-resource course.

courseLedger.name: Living with Water

contentRead.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
contentRead.profile: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
contentRead.topics: Delta environments; Flood risk and protection; Drainage and freshwater management; Sea-level rise and subsidence; Salinization; Water infrastructure and ecological consequences; Water governance, law and justice; Contaminants and pollution; EU Water Framework Directive; Nature-based adaptation; Urban ecology and water; Long-term delta resilience
contentRead.methods: Site-based water-management case analysis; Comparative appraisal of engineered and nature-based solutions; Context-sensitive adaptation-strategy development

courseLedger.contribution: Living with Water examines flood protection, freshwater management, land subsidence and ecological consequences.

courseLedger.name: Computational & Numerical Methods

contentRead.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
contentRead.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
contentRead.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
contentRead.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods

courseLedger.contribution: Computational & Numerical Methods develops numerical modelling, root finding and differential-equation methods.

courseLedger.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry

contentRead.description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
contentRead.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.
contentRead.topics: Natural-water composition; Chemical equilibrium and ionic activity; Aqueous speciation and complexation; Mineral saturation, precipitation and dissolution; Carbonate equilibria, alkalinity and buffering; Ocean acidification; Redox processes and microbial controls; Adsorption and mineral surfaces; Weathering and clay formation; Biomineralization; Contaminant transport; Environmental remediation and resource recovery
contentRead.methods: Geochemical equilibrium and speciation modelling; Geochemist's Workbench; Piper diagrams; Pourbaix and stability diagrams; Laboratory geochemical investigations; Geochemical data interpretation

courseLedger.contribution: Environmental Biogeochemistry uses geochemical modelling to analyse waters, minerals and element cycles.

courseLedger.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta

contentRead.description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
contentRead.profile: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
contentRead.topics: Regionally situated sustainability problems; Research-question development; Research planning; Academic literature and evidence; External stakeholder collaboration; Applied sustainability investigation
contentRead.methods: Literature review; Research design

courseLedger.contribution: Applied research process with a Zeeland sustainability partner: literature,question,investigation andfinalproduct/report. Subject and techniques depend on the project; no guaranteed geological fieldwork or international engineering design.

courseLedger.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation

contentRead.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
contentRead.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
contentRead.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
contentRead.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

courseLedger.contribution: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation applies environmental chemistry and laboratory methods to resource recovery and contamination.

courseLedger.name: Machine Learning

contentRead.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
contentRead.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
contentRead.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
contentRead.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

courseLedger.contribution: Develops regression/classification, resampling, regularisation, trees, support-vector and unsupervised-learning methods with real-data projects. These are complementary methods for environmental/spatial analysis; a dedicated Earth-science dataset or project is not guaranteed.

courseLedger.name: Earth's Resources

contentRead.description2: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.

courseLedger.contribution: Earth’s Resources provides advanced geoscience research on geothermal energy, subsurface carbon storage, nuclear-waste storage and responsible resource use.

courseLedger.name: Governance of Sustainability

contentRead.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
contentRead.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
contentRead.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
contentRead.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

courseLedger.contribution: Governance of Sustainability examines institutions and interests shaping climate adaptation and environmental action.

courseLedger.name: Renewable System Design

contentRead.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

courseLedger.contribution: Renewable System Design develops technical and economic assessment of lower-carbon energy systems through an external-company project.

courseLedger.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works

contentRead.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
contentRead.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
contentRead.topics: Ecology and evolution; Environmental conditions and resources; Climate and life cycles; Ecological niches; Competition and cohabitation; Predation and food webs; Natural selection; Population dynamics; Biodiversity patterns; Ecological succession; Ecosystem energy and matter fluxes; Global cycles; Conservation and human impacts; Ecosystem value
contentRead.methods: Ecological modelling in R; Population-dynamics calculations; Ecosystem energy and matter-flux calculations; Ecological research-project design and analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Ecosystems Uncovered directly examines ecological processes and interactions between organisms and environmental conditions.

courseLedger.name: Linear Algebra

contentRead.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
contentRead.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
contentRead.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
contentRead.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

courseLedger.contribution: Linear Algebra supplies vector and matrix methods used in spatial modelling and data science.

courseLedger.name: Building with Nature

contentRead.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
contentRead.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
contentRead.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
contentRead.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

courseLedger.contribution: Building with Nature examines ecosystem-based design, land reclamation and flood protection.

courseLedger.name: Algorithms & Data Structures

contentRead.description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
contentRead.profile: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
contentRead.topics: Abstract data structures; Asymptotic complexity; Random-number generation and sampling; Sorting and stability; String matching and finite automata; Sequential and binary search; Graph traversal; Shortest paths and spanning trees; Topological sorting; Computability and Turing machines; Polynomial-time verification; Reductions and complexity hierarchy
contentRead.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions

courseLedger.contribution: Algorithms & Data Structures develops efficient computational methods for large and complex datasets.

courseLedger.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision

contentRead.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
contentRead.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
contentRead.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
contentRead.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images

courseLedger.contribution: Specific complementary digital-image representation,filtering,segmentation,feature detection andrecognition usingPython/OpenCV; these computational techniques can support Earth observation,without claiming dedicated remote-sensing acquisition.

courseLedger.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy

contentRead.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
contentRead.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
contentRead.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
contentRead.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

courseLedger.contribution: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy evaluates environmental impacts of technologies and resource use across complete life cycles.

courseLedger.name: Linear Systems

contentRead.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
contentRead.profile: Analyzes continuous- and discrete-time signals and linear time-invariant systems through differential or difference equations, impulse responses and frequency-domain representations. Convolution, Fourier series and transforms lead into sampling and reconstruction, filtering, communication systems, Laplace and Z-transforms, and linear feedback. Mathematica laboratories and an applied project connect mathematical properties to signal processing and system behaviour.
contentRead.topics: Continuous- and discrete-time signals; System linearity, causality and stability; Impulse and frequency responses; Convolution; Fourier series and transforms; Time-frequency representations; Sampling, reconstruction and aliasing; Digital filtering; Modulation and multiplexing; Laplace and Z-transforms; Regions of convergence and pole-zero representations; Linear feedback and stability
contentRead.methods: Convolution sums and integrals; Fourier-series and Fourier-transform analysis; Bode-plot analysis; Sampling and signal reconstruction; Filter analysis; Modulation and demodulation; Laplace and Z-transform analysis; Block-diagram system analysis; Root-locus analysis; Mathematica signal and system computation

courseLedger.contribution: Direct continuous/discrete signal and linear-system methods, Fourier/Laplace/Z transforms,sampling,filtering andfeedback. Complements geophysical sensing; no guaranteed stochastic geoscience time-series or geological model.

courseLedger.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice

contentRead.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

courseLedger.contribution: Social Movements & Environmental Justice examines the justice, participation and conflict dimensions of resource extraction and environmental intervention.
